source: Sinha, Goel, Kumaraguru, Geiping, Bethge, Prabhu (2025) Can Language Models Falsify? REFUTE benchmark
finding: Models that can solve many competitive programming problems can rarely build a counterexample to a subtly wrong solution, even with code execution. Writing a counterexample is much harder than solving.
numbers: Best agent (o3-mini high with code execution feedback) breaks under 9% of incorrect solutions. Its estimated solve rate on the same problems is about 48.7% (rating 2130); DeepSeek-R1 44.0% (rating 2029). 324 problems in the evaluated set (403 after the filters; 152 interactive and 92 low-rated problems were removed earlier). Giving the model the correct solution did not raise the counterexample rate much (zero-shot cells 0.9 to 8.9% across models).
quote: can create counterexamples for only < 9% of incorrect solutions in REFUTE
limits: Algorithmic code, not mathematical conjectures. The counterexample is checked by running code, so the test is clean. The Table 1 text layout was garbled in extraction, so per-model cells beyond the headline are not quoted.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence against assuming that a model that can solve a task can also falsify. A find-a-counterexample step needs its own check and should not be trusted to catch errors by itself.

source: Sinha et al. (2025) REFUTE, randomized search prompting (Table 2)
finding: Explicitly telling the model to write a random input generator plus a brute-force solver and compare outputs gave small gains for chat models and little for reasoning models.
numbers: RandSearch success: DeepSeek-V3 4.0%, Gemini Flash 2.0 Thinking 3.7%, DeepSeek-R1 4.0%, o3-mini (high) 8.3%. With an oracle correct solution (RandSearch Oracle): V3 15.1%, Flash 7.7%, R1 9.9%. For o3-mini the search found counterexamples to 6% of submissions that prompting and agent modes missed (3% when given the correct solution).
limits: Single benchmark; the o3-mini oracle cell is missing in the text. Search time capped at 2 minutes. Problems breakable by search without reasoning were filtered out, which lowers the value of search by design.
agent_relevance: Direct answer to gap 2 for hard cases: brute-force search before proof is not a free win. It adds new coverage (6%) but is capped by the model writing wrong brute-force code.

source: Sinha et al. (2025) REFUTE, failure analysis of search and execution feedback
finding: Most search runs failed because the model wrote wrong brute-force code, not because search is weak. Execution feedback removed invalid-input errors but did not raise true success except for DeepSeek-R1.
numbers: On average 35% of RandSearch runs ended with an incorrect counterexample; of these 14% were test-validation errors and 86% were wrong brute-force code. Flash and o3-mini were bottlenecked about equally (28% vs 32% of all samples). Execution feedback removed all validation failures for R1 and V3 (45 and 36 failures at zero-shot). The ReAct agent allowed up to 10 code runs and 5 resubmits.
limits: Only DeepSeek-R1 showed modest gains from execution feedback. Success was not predictable from problem difficulty or submission traits (hacked subset 4% +/- 1%).
agent_relevance: A code sandbox helps input validity, so the checking code itself needs a cross-check (for example run on tiny known cases) before its negative result is trusted.

source: Balunovic, Dekoninck, Petrov, Jovanovic, Vechev (2025) MathConstruct: challenging LLM reasoning with constructive proofs (code agents)
finding: Giving models a Python interpreter (up to 4 runs) on construction problems roughly doubled accuracy at about five times the cost, but accuracy stayed low.
numbers: 121 problems, 456 instances; best base model about 60% (later footnote: GPT-5 high 82.0%). With code: most models roughly double; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 5% to 18%; Gemini Flash best at 20%. Cost up about 5x.
limits: Constructive problems with an automatic verifier, not proofs of general statements. Sandbox with numpy, scipy, sympy. Numbers are for older 2025 models.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 2: code execution gives a large relative gain on construction and answer-finding tasks, but from a very low base, and it costs tokens. Without a sandbox that gain is not available.

source: Balunovic et al. (2025) MathConstruct, brute-force agents (Table 3)
finding: Pure brute force solves under 10% of construction problems. Brute-forcing small cases and then generalizing the pattern did better and beat the plain code agent.
numbers: GPT-4o: BRUTE 7.64 (robust 1.65) vs BRUTE+INFER 12.88 (robust 4.13). Claude 3.5 Sonnet: BRUTE 9.92 (robust 2.48) vs BRUTE+INFER 19.21 (robust 6.61). BRUTE+INFER allowed 3 refinements with parser feedback.
quote: frequently discovers patterns by generalizing from smaller instances
limits: Robust accuracy means all variants of a problem solved. The authors kept the problems brute-force inference solved, since this counts as real reasoning.
agent_relevance: Supports the small-cases-then-generalize order of the conjecture step: compute, spot a pattern, then prove. Search alone is not enough.

source: Guo, Xie, Liu, Huang et al. (2026) Code2Math: can your code agent evolve math problems through exploration? (solvability)
finding: A code agent can rewrite seed problems into new, harder, solvable ones, but a share of its own variants are flawed even after an internal solvability check. An independent judge catches the rest.
numbers: 100 seed problems, up to 20 rollouts each. The external judge (GPT-5.2-high) certified between 74 of 90 and 98 of 98 internally accepted problems depending on the evolver (DeepSeek-Chat 83/94, DeepSeek-Reasoner 94/98, Gemini-3-Pro 98/98, Kimi-K2 74/90, Seed-2.0-Pro 83/97). So up to 18% of internally accepted variants were rejected by the second check.
limits: The judge is an LLM. Human audit: 126 of 127 judge-valid problems were valid (99.2%). That checks precision of the judge, not recall of invalid problems.
agent_relevance: Direct answer to gap 8: a solver's own variants are sometimes ill-posed (0 to 18% rejected by an independent check after a self-check), so what-if-not variants need an independent solvability check.

source: Guo et al. (2026) Code2Math, difficulty and training utility
finding: Evolved problems are harder (lower solve rate, more tokens), and adding them to SFT data raised AIME scores.
numbers: GPT-5.2-High drops from 70% on seeds to 64% (DeepSeek-Reasoner evolutions) and 61% (Gemini-3-Pro and Seed-2.0-Pro evolutions); Gemini-3-Flash drops up to 32 points; DeepSeek-Chat on Gemini evolutions 16 to 7. Median tokens 9,606 original vs 11,434 to 17,277 evolved. SFT Avg@10 on AIME24/25/26: Qwen3-8B 39.9% to 44.4% (+4.5), Qwen3-14B 55.6% to 60.2% (+4.7).
limits: Training result is one SFT run per size, no seeds or error bars in the text read. Training corpus 2,500 problems. Judge is GPT-5.2-high.
agent_relevance: Shows self-posed harder variants can carry signal in natural language, unlike the formal-only evidence in earlier files. A training result does not transfer to an inference-only scaffold.

source: Guo et al. (2026) Code2Math, human audit and failure after evolution
finding: Human audit supports the LLM judge. Many solvers that solved the seed fail the evolved version, so evolution truly changes the solution pattern.
numbers: Judge-valid: 126/127 human-valid (99.2%). Solver-answer agreement 1134/1226 (92.5%). Difficulty exact agreement 79.3% (115/145), within one point 95.9%. 35 olympiad-seed problems: 34/35 improved by both human and GPT. Failure-after-evolution 166 of 338 solver-problem pairs (49.1%); Gemini-3-Pro evolutions 61.8%.
limits: Audit by one mathematics postgraduate (olympiad subset also by a postdoc). Only judge-valid problems analysed.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a variant generator plus a verifier pair is usable in natural language, at several rollouts per kept problem. Cost, not validity, is the limit.

source: Li, Kuang, Huang, Xu et al. (2025) One example shown, many concepts known: CounterMATH (ICML 2025)
finding: Benchmark of 1,216 university-level statement and rationale pairs where the answer needs a counterexample. Most models judge truth poorly and rarely give examples.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1 F1 (macro) 80.7; Qwen2.5-Math-72B-Instruct 41.8; most open-source 7B models about 30 F1 (DeepSeek-Math-7B-rl 32.2). Examples-given rate ranges 18.3% to 74.2%; strict example-use rate for Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct 30.2% (some models 0.4%). Judge-model agreement with humans 93.5%; annotator agreement 95.4%.
limits: Truth judgement is binary so chance level is high; example matching uses LLM and lexical checks. Many open models give almost no real counterexamples.
agent_relevance: Counterexample use is a known weak point. Supports forcing an explicit try-to-build-a-counterexample step with a check.

source: Li et al. (2025) CounterMATH, fine-tuning and out-of-distribution transfer
finding: SFT on 1,025 counterexample samples slightly raised the in-domain score and gave larger gains on other math sets, but it is a training result.
numbers: In-domain Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct: F1 38.3 base, 39.4 with SFT, 41.1 with SFT plus hint prompt (as read from the table; hint prompt alone 39.7 vs 38.3). OOD base 7B: GSM8K 95.1, MATH 80.5, OlympiadBench 41.6, MMLU-college-math 74.0, AIME24 20.0; after SFT 95.6, 87.9, 46.4, 80.0, 30.0 (AIME24 is 30 problems, so +10 points is 3 problems).
limits: One run, no variance. The extracted table rows were scrambled, so the row assignment is read from row order. The hint prompt alone added little.
agent_relevance: A prompt hint to reason by example added at most about 1.4 F1. The scaffold effect from a counterexample hint alone is small.

source: Li, Li, Yang, Ma, Su (2026) Learning to disprove: formal counterexample generation with LLMs (rejected from ICLR 2026)
finding: Training a Qwen3 8B with a symbolic mutation recipe (remove a hypothesis from a proved theorem so it becomes false) improves formal disproving in Lean.
numbers: 575K counterexample instances, 3K validation. Multi-reward at convergence pass@1/4/9 about 49/52/54% vs single-reward 43/46/47%. On three benchmarks it solves 95, 69 and 63 more problems at pass@1 than the strongest baseline.
limits: Formal Lean only; training based; benchmarks collected by the authors, and the paper says existing benchmarks contain inaccuracies. Paper was rejected from ICLR 2026.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis deletion is a cheap way to make false variants; it matches the what-if-not step of dropping a given. It is evidence the move yields usable tasks, not evidence about prompting.

source: Allamanis and Yin (2025) Disproving program equivalence with LLMs (ProbeGen)
finding: An LLM that proposes inputs and sees execution output can find counterexamples that benchmark unit tests missed.
numbers: Disproves 18% of samples that the benchmark unit tests judged equivalent to ground truth. Using the probes to cluster semantically equal samples raised pass@1 by 10% (as stated in the abstract).
limits: Code, not mathematics; abstract and introduction read, not the full tables.
agent_relevance: Execution-guided probing is cheap and finds real defects; clustering by probes shows a test-then-vote pattern.

source: Zhang, Stylianides and Stylianides (2024) Enhancing mathematical problem posing competence: a meta-analysis of intervention studies. Int. J. STEM Education
finding: Newer meta-analysis of 26 problem-posing intervention studies (1996 to 2021). The mean effect is medium and positive, but the outcome is problem-posing skill, not solving accuracy.
numbers: 1,412 records screened, 509 full text, 26 studies (31 effect sizes). Random effects without one outlier (g = 3.32 removed): g = 0.72, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.90, p < 0.001, 30 effect sizes from 25 studies. Heterogeneity Q(29)=94.25, I2=69.2%. Meta-regression R2 = 0.68.
limits: Outcomes are quantity and quality of posed problems and attitudes, not later test scores. 13 studies K-12, 10 prospective teachers, 3 in-service. 9 studies lasted under 1 day.
agent_relevance: Puts the likely human posing effect at about 0.5 to 0.9 on posing skill, a bit lower than the earlier g 0.64-1.31. Not evidence for solving gains.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) meta-analysis, moderators and publication bias
finding: Effects shrink with controlled designs and with older participants, and the funnel plot is asymmetric.
numbers: Pre-post designs gave on average 58% larger effect than pre-post-control designs (p < 0.1). K-12 students gained 89% more than prospective teachers and 96% more than in-service teachers (p < 0.001 and p < 0.01). Egger test significant (p < 0.05, asymmetric funnel); trim-and-fill and the meta-regression test (z=1.719, p>0.05) found not enough evidence of publication bias. Authors say bias may still exist.
limits: What-if-not appears only as one example of a strategy component; no WIN-only effect size is reported. Many studies are short and use researcher-made tests.
agent_relevance: Answers part of gap 7: with controls the effect is smaller, and no study isolates What-If-Not. Guided reinvention (Larsen and Zandieh) was not re-checked, so that part of gap 7 stays open.

source: Liu, Yin, Yuan et al. (2026) Discover and Prove: Hard Mode automated theorem proving in Lean 4 (ACL 2026)
finding: When the answer is given in the formal statement (Easy Mode) systems look far better than when they must find it first (Hard Mode). Guessing the answer in natural language is much easier than proving it formally.
numbers: State-of-the-art LLMs exceed 80% answer accuracy on PutnamBench problems where formal provers manage under 10%. DAP formally proves 36 PutnamBench theorems in Hard Mode and raises CombiBench from 7 to 10 solved. Discovery module PutnamBench answers: 293 of 340 (86%) with agent self-verification vs 265 (78%) without.
limits: Formal Lean setting. Answer correctness checked against ground truth only on problems with a definitive answer. Pass@32.
agent_relevance: Data for gaps 5 and 10: hiding the answer is a large change in difficulty (same direction as ConjectureBench), and models are good at natural-language answer discovery on Putnam-type problems.

source: Liu et al. (2026) Discover and Prove, ablations and leaked-answer proofs
finding: Self-verification rounds help only on hard sets. Leaving the answer visible in the statement lets models cheat with trivial proofs.
numbers: Self-verification iterations (0, 5, 10, 30) on PutnamBench (340): 265, 291, 292, 293. FIMO-Hard (70): 38, 40, 43, 43. CombiBench (45): 29, 31, 32, 32. miniF2F-Hard (194): 194 at every setting (saturation, possible contamination).
quote: We frequently observed spurious proofs (cheating behavior)
limits: Pass@32. Authors suggest contamination for miniF2F. Spurious proofs closed by rfl because the answer abbreviation equalled the target set.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 partly closed: leaving the target visible changes scores in two ways, easier and with cheating. Our own benchmark prompts need a leakage check.

source: Baba, Liu, Kurita, Sannai (2026) Prover Agent: an agent-based framework for formal mathematical proofs (v5)
finding: Training-free inference-time agent that, when direct proving fails, writes auxiliary lemmas (special cases and useful facts, not only subgoals) with an informal LLM, proves them in Lean, and feeds the verified ones back.
numbers: 88.1% on miniF2F-test with 260 samples (ensemble of Goedel-Prover-V2 and DeepSeek-Prover-V2; 64.3% at one sample), 25 PutnamBench problems. Of the lemmas used in successful proofs (Table 5): 25.0% special cases, 25.0% technique-inducing, 41.7% effective subgoals, 8.3% failed to prove, 0% inserted unchanged.
limits: Formal Lean. Lemma category numbers come from a small sample (percentages imply 12 lemmas). Lemma value cannot be separated from extra samples; the paper plots pass rate against sample budget.
agent_relevance: Closest inference-time test for gap 6: lemmas that are special cases matter as much as subgoals. No pass-rate filter is used, so the STP filter at inference remains untested.

source: Ota, Osa and Harada (2026) Self-supervised theorem discovery in a formal axiomatic system
finding: An agent that grows a theorem library from axioms alone finds proofs for 30% of human benchmark problems, and handing the discovered theorems to GPT models as prompt lemmas raised their proof rate.
numbers: GPT-5-high baseline about 23% on the Hilbert-system benchmark; agent 30%. Prompt-lemma gain shown for GPT-4o and GPT-5 variants in Figure 6 (no exact values in the text). Tens of thousands of theorems discovered.
limits: Propositional Hilbert system only, single-shot, values only in a figure. Authors say they do not claim to beat state-of-the-art LLMs.
agent_relevance: Partial support for gap 3: a library of verified results given as context helps a different model, in a toy formal system. Not a natural-language test and not a replication of CPL 5/20 vs 0/20.

source: Gap search log: no study found for What-If-Not on LLMs, Lakatos moves on LLMs, CPL on a second target, or an inference-time pass-rate filter
finding: Targeted web searches (6 returned results; the last 2 were refused for shared budget) found no paper testing What-If-Not or Lakatos counterexample moves on a language model, no replication of CPL on a second target, and no inference-time pass-rate lemma filter. Search results only, no page opened for the negative claim.
numbers: Searches: what-if-not or Lakatos plus LLM (no hit); code counterexample search (REFUTE, MathConstruct, ProbeGen found); CPL replication (only CPL itself, v2 May 2026, NALOMA 2026); human posing meta-analyses (Zhang 2024 found); answer-first (DAP found); inference lemma filtering (Prover Agent and 2606.28747 found). arXiv, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar APIs returned HTTP 429.
limits: Absence of a hit in a rate-limited search is weak evidence of absence. Gaps 1, 3 (replication), 4 and 6 stay open.
agent_relevance: These are untested; to answer them we must run the experiment ourselves (small, equal-token A/B).
